content: One potential approach to improving outcomes for pregnant or postpartum women with drug or alcohol problems is the implementation of home visits. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of home visits during pregnancy and/or after birth for women with substance use issues. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO, up to November 30, 2011. Additional sources included citations from previous reviews, trials, and expert consultations. The inclusion criteria for the studies were randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving pregnant or postpartum women with drug or alcohol problems. Trials that enrolled high-risk women, where more than 50% were reported to use drugs or alcohol, were also considered eligible. The review authors independently assessed the trials and performed statistical analyses using fixed-effect and random-effects models, as appropriate. Seven studies, involving a total of 803 mother-infant pairs, were included in the analysis. These studies primarily compared home visits conducted after birth with no home visits. The individuals conducting the home visits included community health nurses, pediatric nurses, trained counselors, paraprofessional advocates, midwives, and lay African-American women. However, several of these studies had significant methodological limitations. The results showed no significant differences in several key outcomes between women who received home visits and those who did not. These outcomes included continued illicit drug use (three studies, 384 women; risk ratio [RR] 1.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89 to 1.24), continued alcohol use (three studies, 379 women; RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.46), failure to enroll in a drug treatment program (two studies, 211 women; RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.94), and not breastfeeding at six months (two studies, 260 infants; RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.10). Similarly, there were no significant differences in the rates of incomplete six-month infant vaccination schedules (two studies, 260 infants; RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32), scores on the Bayley Mental Development Index (three studies, 199 infants; mean difference [MD] 2.89, 95% CI -1.17 to 6.95) or Psychomotor Index (MD 3.14, 95% CI -0.03 to 6.32), child behavioral problems (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.01), infants not in the care of their biological mother (two studies, 254 infants; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.39), non-accidental injury and non-voluntary foster care (two studies, 254 infants; RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.23), or infant death (three studies, 288 infants; RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.12 to 4.16). However, individual studies did report some significant findings. Specifically, there was a reduction in involvement with child protective services (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.74) and a reduction in failure to use postpartum contraception (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.82). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of home visits for pregnant or postpartum women with drug or alcohol problems. They emphasized the need for further large, high-quality trials to better evaluate the potential benefits of this intervention.
